title: Google Cloud Partner Advantage Tiers, Explained
summary: How Google Cloud Partner Advantage is structured: the engagement models, the tiers, and what marketplace plus co-sell benefits each one unlocks for ISVs.
body_markdown:
*Google Cloud Partner Advantage is Google Cloud’s partner program, organized as engagement models you choose by how you work with Google — Sell, Build, Services — each carrying tiers (Member, Partner, Premier) that unlock progressively more marketplace and co-sell support. It is not a single ranked ladder; the model decides what you get access to, and the tier decides how much.*


---


An alliances leader joining a Google Cloud motion usually inherits one confused sentence: “we need to hit Premier.” It is the wrong shape for the question. Partner Advantage is not a single ladder you climb from bottom to top — it is a small set of engagement models, and *which model you are in* matters as much as *what tier you reach* inside it. Aiming at “Premier” without naming the model is like aiming at “senior” without naming the job.


This is the structure, described so you can locate yourself in it before you commit a quarter of partner-ops time to advancing. It is built from how Google itself frames the program, and it deliberately states no revenue thresholds, certification counts, or fees — those are the numbers Google revises each year, and an alliances plan built on last year’s figure ages the day Google updates the page.


---


## What is Google Cloud Partner Advantage?


**Google Cloud Partner Advantage is Google Cloud’s partner program, structured around engagement models a partner chooses to match how it works with Google — rather than one ranked track everyone shares.** Google organizes the program by *motion* first: a partner that resells and transacts Google Cloud is in a different model from one that builds software on Google Cloud, which is different again from one that delivers services. You select the model that describes what you actually do, and the program’s benefits are scoped to that model.


The key idea is that the model is the primary axis, not a rung. Two partners can both be “in Partner Advantage” and have almost nothing in common, because they entered through different engagement models aimed at different outcomes. For an ISV selling software on Google Cloud, the relevant model is the one built around selling and transacting — which is where the[Google Cloud Marketplace](https://www.suger.io/solutions/gcp-marketplace/) motion sits. Everything an ISV cares about (marketplace listing support, co-sell access, incentives) flows from being in the right model first, and only then from the tier you reach within it.


---


## The engagement models — pick the one that describes your motion


**An engagement model is Partner Advantage’s way of asking “how do you work with Google Cloud?” before it asks “how far have you progressed?”** Google frames the program around a few distinct motions, and a partner can be active in more than one. The three that matter to most software companies are these.


- **Sell.** For partners that resell, distribute, or transact Google Cloud — the motion that includes selling your product through Google Cloud Marketplace and co-selling with the Google field. If you are an ISV listing software and want it bought against a customer’s Google commitment, this is your model.
- **Build.** For partners that build software or a service *on* Google Cloud — technology partners whose product runs on or integrates with Google Cloud. An ISV frequently qualifies here for the technical relationship even while it engages the Sell motion for the commercial one.
- **Services.** For partners that deliver consulting, implementation, or managed services on Google Cloud. This is the SI/consulting motion, distinct from selling a product of your own.


The practical consequence: **an ISV usually lives in more than one model at once** — Build for the technical partnership, Sell for the marketplace and co-sell motion — and the benefits you care about attach to the *right* model for each goal. Do not evaluate “what tier are we?” in the abstract. Ask “in which model, for which motion?” A strong Build standing does not, by itself, unlock the Sell-side incentives, and vice versa.


---


## The tiers inside a model — Member, Partner, Premier


**Within an engagement model, Partner Advantage recognizes progressively higher tiers — Member, Partner, and Premier — where each higher tier requires demonstrated capability and unlocks more support.** This is the ladder people mean when they say “Premier,” but it only makes sense *inside a named model* . Premier in the Sell model and Premier in the Services model are different achievements with different requirements.


The shape of the progression is consistent even though the specifics differ by model:


- **Member** is the entry standing — you have joined the model and can access its foundational benefits and enablement. It is where you establish the relationship and start building the evidence higher tiers ask for.
- **Partner** is the mid tier, earned by demonstrating real capability and, in the Sell motion, real transacting activity. It is where meaningful co-sell engagement and marketplace support typically become available.
- **Premier** is the top tier, reserved for partners that have demonstrated the highest level of capability, investment, and results in that model. It carries the most support and the most visible recognition — and the most stringent, periodically re-evaluated requirements.


Two honest cautions. First, **the requirements to reach and hold each tier — revenue transacted, specializations or certifications earned, and any fees — are current-year figures Google publishes and revises** , so this post names none of them; check Google’s own become-a-partner page for the number that applies when you are reading. Second, **tiers are re-evaluated periodically** , so a tier is a standing you maintain, not a badge you keep forever. Plan for the renewal, not just the attainment.


---


## What each engagement model and tier unlocks


**Partner Advantage benefits scale on two axes at once: the engagement model decides *which kinds* of benefit you can access, and the tier decides *how much* .** The table below is the mental model — what a motion unlocks in principle, held deliberately free of any threshold that would age. Read it as “which door,” not “how many dollars.”


Engagement model / tier What the motion is for What it unlocks for an ISV, in principle


**Sell — Member** Establishing the transacting relationship Ability to begin listing and transacting on Google Cloud Marketplace; foundational sell-side enablement


**Sell — Partner** Demonstrated transacting and co-sell capability Fuller marketplace support and access to co-sell engagement with the Google field


**Sell — Premier** Top-tier transacting partner The most marketplace and co-sell support, strongest field visibility, and highest recognition


**Build — Member → Premier** Technical partnership; product on Google Cloud Technical enablement and integration recognition; validation that your product runs on Google Cloud, scaling with tier


**Services — Member → Premier** Consulting/implementation delivery Delivery enablement and services recognition, scaling with tier


Two readings keep this from becoming a wish list. First, **every entry is access or standing, not booked revenue** — reaching Sell Partner opens the co-sell door; it does not deposit pipeline. The value is realized only when you actually run the motion the tier unlocks, which is exactly what an operational[co-sell workflow](https://www.suger.io/platform/cosell/) is for. Second, **the marketplace and co-sell benefits an ISV wants concentrate in the Sell model** , which is why “we’re a Build partner, so we’re covered” is a common and costly misread — the Build standing earns you the technical relationship, not the sell-side incentives.


---


## Where marketplace and co-sell actually connect


**Marketplace transacting and Google co-sell are the two Sell-model benefits an ISV builds a Google plan around — and they reinforce each other.** A Google Cloud Marketplace listing is how your product is sold and metered on Google Cloud, and it is also what makes a deal *co-sellable* : a transaction the Google field can be credited for is the raw material of the co-sell motion. Progressing your Sell tier is, in effect, progressing your standing in both at once.


That is why the sequencing matters. The listing is the prerequisite the co-sell motion plugs into, not a parallel effort — a point covered end to end in the[Google Cloud Marketplace ISV seller guide](https://www.suger.io/resources/blog/google-cloud-marketplace-isv-seller-guide/) . And because co-sell is where higher Sell tiers pay off, the[alliances and partnerships](https://www.suger.io/solutions/alliances-partnerships/) function is the one that turns a tier into revenue: the tier grants access to the Google field, and the alliances motion is what converts that access into sourced and influenced deals. A tier with no motion behind it is a badge; a motion with no tier behind it is cold outreach.


---


## Frequently asked questions


**What is Google Cloud Partner Advantage?** Google Cloud Partner Advantage is Google Cloud’s partner program. It is organized around engagement models a partner chooses to match how it works with Google — Sell, Build, or Services — each with tiers that unlock progressively more support. It is not a single ranked ladder everyone shares.


**What are the Google Cloud Partner Advantage tiers?** Within an engagement model, the tiers rise from Member to Partner to Premier. Each higher tier requires more demonstrated capability and unlocks more support. Because tiers exist inside a model, Premier in the Sell motion is a different achievement from Premier in Services.


**Which Partner Advantage model does an ISV selling on Google Cloud Marketplace need?** The Sell model, which covers transacting on Google Cloud Marketplace and co-selling with the Google field. Many ISVs are also in the Build model for the technical partnership, but the marketplace and co-sell benefits attach to Sell, not Build.


**What do higher Partner Advantage tiers unlock for marketplace and co-sell?** Higher Sell-model tiers unlock fuller Google Cloud Marketplace support, access to co-sell engagement with the Google field, and stronger visibility and recognition. Each benefit is access or standing, not booked revenue — it pays off only when you run the motion it unlocks.


**What are the revenue or certification requirements for each Partner Advantage tier?** Google publishes tier requirements — such as transacted revenue, specializations or certifications, and any fees — as current-year figures it revises periodically. Check Google’s become-a-partner page for the numbers in effect when you read, rather than relying on a quoted figure that ages.


**Is a Partner Advantage tier permanent once earned?** No. Tiers are re-evaluated periodically, so a tier is a standing you maintain rather than a badge you keep. Plan for the renewal criteria, not only the initial attainment, so you do not slip a tier at re-evaluation.


---


## Takeaways


- Partner Advantage is organized by **engagement model first, tier second** . “Which model, for which motion?” is the question — “are we Premier?” is meaningless without it.
- The three models that matter to software companies are **Sell** (transact and co-sell), **Build** (product on Google Cloud), and **Services** (consulting). An ISV usually lives in more than one at once.
- Inside a model, tiers rise **Member → Partner → Premier** , each requiring more demonstrated capability and unlocking more support — and each **re-evaluated periodically** , so a tier is maintained, not kept.
- The marketplace and co-sell benefits an ISV wants concentrate in the **Sell model** ; a strong Build standing earns the technical relationship, not the sell-side incentives.
- Tier requirements — revenue, certifications, fees — are **current-year figures Google revises** . Read them off Google’s become-a-partner page; don’t build an alliances plan on a number that ages.
